quote: I am no bird; and no net ensnares me: I am a free human being with an independent will; which I now exert to leave you.
source: Charlotte Brontë, Jane Eyre, vol. II, ch. 8 (ch. 23), the orchard at Thornfield (Jane Eyre) (Smith, Elder, 1847)
speaker: Jane Eyre
note: Corrected: the proposal cut the sentence short and closed it with a full stop no edition prints. The 1847 Smith, Elder first edition, volume II, chapter VIII, runs on to which I now exert to leave you, with a semicolon before it. The whole sentence is restored.

evidence.where: The 1847 Smith, Elder first edition, volume II, was downloaded from the Internet Archive as searchable OCR text and read. Its chapter VIII prints: I am no bird; and no net ensnares me: I am a free human being with an independent will; which I now exert to leave you. It answers Rochester's Jane, be still; don't struggle so, like a wild, frantic bird that is rending its own plumage in its desperation, and is followed by Another effort set me at liberty, and I stood erect before him. Counting the chapter headings in that volume places the passage in chapter VIII, which is chapter 23 of the novel. The Lit2Go text, which cites the same 1847 Smith, Elder printing, and the Project Gutenberg text agree on the words, though both close the second clause with a comma where the first edition sets a semicolon.
evidence.edition: Jane Eyre: An Autobiography, vol. II (Smith, Elder, and Co., 1847), first edition
evidence.locator: vol. II, ch. VIII (ch. 23), the orchard at Thornfield, Jane to Rochester

reason: The line is Jane's and stands where the proposal says, and the colon after ensnares me is the first edition's own. What was wrong is the wording: the proposal stopped at independent will and supplied a terminal stop that no edition prints, so the whole sentence is restored as the 1847 text sets it. Shipped.js reports the line unshipped and Brontë at one of three and unbanned. For the editor: 07-poet-16 is also Charlotte Brontë, and only one line per person may stand in a month.
